Two layers here. The indigenous names - Quechua in the north-west
(Jujuy, Catamarca, Tucumán), Mapuche/Tehuelche in the south (Neuquén,
Chubut, Chaco) - are usually about water or landscape. The Spanish ones
are saints, kings and homesick transplants: La Rioja, Córdoba and
Santa Fe are all named after places in Spain.
Ids drop the accents and the ñ, so Neuquén is 'neuquen' and Tucumán is
jujuy: From the name of a local chief or a Quechua term recorded by the Spanish as Xuxuy; the exact meaning is lost.
The Quebrada de Humahuaca running through it was an Inca road and is a UNESCO site; the Hill of Seven Colours at Purmamarca is its picture.
The most Andean province, where more people speak Quechua and Aymara than anywhere else in the country.
salta: Probably from Aymara sallta, "beautiful" — and the province's nickname is Salta la linda, Salta the beautiful.
The Tren a las Nubes climbs to 4,220 m on a viaduct across a gorge, one of the highest railways in the world.
Cafayate here grows torrontés, the white grape Argentina makes better than anyone, at 1,700 m.
formosa: Portuguese and old Spanish for "beautiful" — the same word that named Taiwan, given to a bend in the Paraguay river.
The hottest province: over 45 °C is normal, and its western half is dry thorn scrub.
The Bañado La Estrella, a flooded plain of drowned trees, is one of the largest wetlands in South America.
chaco: From Quechua chaku, a communal hunt in which animals were driven together — the word for the whole Gran Chaco plain.
Its quebracho trees gave the world its tannin for leather, and the logging emptied much of the forest.
One of the poorest provinces, and home to the Qom, Wichí and Mocoví peoples.
misiones: Named for the Jesuit missions: thirty reductions built here from 1609, where Guaraní converts lived under Jesuit rule until Spain expelled the order in 1767.
The ruins of San Ignacio Miní are a UNESCO site, and the story was filmed as The Mission.
Iguazú falls are here — 275 separate drops, and the surrounding rainforest is the largest remnant of the Atlantic forest left.
tucuman: Probably from a Quechua or local phrase meaning "where the yuchán tree grows", or the name of a chief.
The smallest province and the most densely populated, called the garden of the republic; it grows most of Argentina's lemons — and Argentina is the world's largest exporter.
Argentina's independence was declared in the city of San Miguel de Tucumán on 9 July 1816.
catamarca: From Quechua, most likely "fortress on the slope" — cata, a slope, and marca, a settlement or fort.
Its Antofagasta de la Sierra is desert at 3,500 m, with volcanoes, salt flats and almost nobody.
It produces most of Argentina's lithium, alongside Salta and Jujuy, from brine under the salt pans.
santiago-del-estero: "Saint James of the lagoon" — of the estero, the marsh, to tell it from every other Santiago in the Spanish empire.
The oldest continuously inhabited Spanish city in Argentina, founded 1553.
Quichua, the local form of Quechua, is still spoken here, cut off from the Andean varieties by hundreds of kilometres.
corrientes: From the currents — the city was founded in 1588 at a stretch of the Paraná called the seven currents.
The Iberá wetlands here are the second largest in South America after the Pantanal, and jaguars and giant anteaters have been reintroduced.
Chamamé, its accordion music, is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list, and Guaraní is co-official in the province.
la-rioja: Named by a governor after his own home region in Spain — so Argentina's La Rioja is the Spanish one's namesake, not its rival.
Talampaya here is a canyon of red sandstone holding some of the world's oldest dinosaur fossils, from 230 million years ago.
It is dry enough that its vineyards depend entirely on Andean meltwater channelled down from the mountains.
san-juan: For St John the Baptist, on whose feast the valley was claimed in 1562.
The Ischigualasto valley in it, called the Valley of the Moon, produced the first known dinosaurs, Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus.
It is the second wine province after Mendoza and gets about 300 days of sun a year.
santa-fe: "Holy faith", named in 1573 after Santa Fe in Granada, the camp from which Spain took the last Moorish city.
Rosario in it is where the Argentine flag was first raised, and where both Che Guevara and Lionel Messi were born.
The Paraná running along it carries Argentina's grain exports; most of the country's soy leaves through its ports.
entre-rios: "Between rivers" — it lies between the Paraná and the Uruguay, and is almost an island.
Its palm savanna at El Palmar protects the yatay palm, which was nearly cleared for farmland.
Argentina's first constitution was drafted at Santa Fe by a coalition led from here, and the province was the seat of the Argentine Confederation in the 1850s.
cordoba: Named in 1573 after Córdoba in Spain, by a founder whose family came from there.
Its university, founded 1613, is the oldest in Argentina and the fourth oldest in the Americas.
The Jesuit block and estancias around it are a UNESCO site, and the sierras make it the country's inland holiday region.
san-luis: For St Louis, Louis IX of France, whose feast fell near the founding in 1594.
It passed a law giving every resident free wireless internet, unusually early, in 2007.
Its Sierra de las Quijadas is a red rock national park with dinosaur and pterosaur tracks.
ciudad-de-buenos-aires: "Good airs" — short for Santa María del Buen Ayre, a Sardinian shrine the sailors who founded it prayed to.
It has more bookshops per head than any other city in the world, and its Teatro Colón is ranked among the best opera houses for acoustics.
Tango was born in its port districts in the 1880s, among immigrants and dockworkers, and was disreputable for decades before Paris made it fashionable.
mendoza: For García Hurtado de Mendoza, the governor of Chile who ordered the city founded in 1561.
It makes about 70% of Argentina's wine, and malbec — a minor grape in France — became its own here.
Aconcagua on its border is the highest mountain outside Asia at 6,961 m, and its whole irrigation system is Inca in origin.
buenos-aires: The province around the capital, sharing its name but administered separately — the city is a district of its own.
The pampas here are some of the most fertile grassland on earth, and the beef and grain from them made Argentina briefly one of the world's richest countries.
The gaucho tradition comes from this plain, and Martín Fierro, the national poem, is about one.
la-pampa: From Quechua pampa, "a flat plain" — a word that has entered English for this grassland.
It was taken from the Mapuche in the Conquest of the Desert campaign of 1878–85, which killed or displaced most of the people living here.
Its Lihué Calel hills are the only relief for hundreds of kilometres in any direction.
neuquen: From Mapudungun newenken, "bold" or "forceful", the name of the river.
Vaca Muerta under it is one of the largest shale oil and gas fields in the world.
Its Valle de los Dinosaurios yielded Argentinosaurus and Giganotosaurus — among the largest herbivore and carnivore ever found.
rio-negro: "Black river", for the dark water of the river formed where the Limay and the Neuquén meet.
Bariloche in it was settled by Germans, Swiss and Austrians, which is why an Andean town makes chocolate and looks Alpine.
Its valley grows most of Argentina's apples and pears, irrigated from the river.
chubut: From Tehuelche chupat, "transparent" — the clear water of the Chubut river.
A Welsh colony settled here in 1865 to keep their language, and Welsh is still spoken in Gaiman and Trelew.
Península Valdés on its coast is a UNESCO site where southern right whales calve and orcas beach themselves to take sea lions.
santa-cruz: "Holy cross", named by Magellan's expedition for the day it anchored in the estuary in 1520.
The Cueva de las Manos holds stencilled handprints painted 9,000 years ago, the oldest art in South America.
Perito Moreno glacier here is one of the few in the world that is not retreating, and it calves into a lake with a roar.
tierra-del-fuego: "Land of fire" — Magellan saw the fires the Yaghan kept burning on shore and named the land for them.
Ushuaia calls itself the southernmost city in the world, and the Beagle Channel through it is named for Darwin's ship.
The Yaghan lived here naked in near-freezing weather, kept warm by fires and seal grease; the last native speaker of their language died in 2022.
san-salvador-de-jujuy: "Holy Saviour of Jujuy" — the saint plus the province name, which is of lost indigenous origin.
It was founded three times, the first two attempts destroyed by the Omaguaca people.
Belgrano ordered the whole population to evacuate and burn everything in 1812, the Jujuy Exodus, to deny the Spanish supplies.
posadas: Named for Gervasio Antonio de Posadas, an early head of state of the United Provinces.
It faces Encarnación in Paraguay across the Paraná, joined by a bridge.
The Jesuit mission ruins of San Ignacio Miní, a UNESCO site, are in its province.
resistencia: Spanish for "resistance", named for settlers who held out against attacks while founding it in 1878.
It has over 600 sculptures in its streets and calls itself the city of statues.
It sits opposite Corrientes across the Paraná, joined by a suspension bridge.
concordia: Latin for "harmony" — a hopeful name given at its founding in 1832.
It is the centre of Argentina’s citrus industry, especially mandarins and blood oranges.
The Salto Grande dam nearby is shared with Uruguay and drowned the falls the town was named after.
parana: From Tupi pará-nã, "like the sea" — the river is wide enough to deserve it.
It was the capital of the Argentine Confederation from 1853 to 1861.
A tunnel under the river joins it to Santa Fe, one of the first underwater road tunnels in South America.
rosario: For the Virgin of the Rosary — the city has no formal founding date or founder, unusually.
The Argentine flag was first raised here by Belgrano in 1812, and a vast monument marks the spot.
Che Guevara and Lionel Messi were both born in the city.
san-martin: Named for José de San Martín, who led the liberation of Argentina, Chile and Peru.
He crossed the Andes in 1817 with 5,000 men and their artillery, a feat compared to Hannibal’s.
General San Martín is part of Greater Buenos Aires and an industrial centre.
rio-cuarto: "Fourth river" — Spanish surveyors numbered the rivers crossing the pampa rather than naming them.
It was a frontier fort against the Ranquel people and is now Córdoba province’s second city.
It sits at the centre of Argentina’s soy and peanut belt.
san-nicolas: For St Nicholas of Bari — San Nicolás de los Arroyos, "of the streams".
The San Nicolás Agreement of 1852 here set the terms for Argentina’s constitution.
Its steelworks was the country’s first integrated mill, opened in 1960.
san-rafael: It is the second city of Mendoza province and makes a large share of Argentina’s wine and preserved fruit.
The Atuel canyon nearby is a gorge of coloured rock used for rafting and climbing.
la-plata: "The silver" — from the Río de la Plata, named by Spaniards hoping for silver they never found there.
Built from nothing in 1882 as a planned capital for Buenos Aires province, on a perfect square grid with diagonals.
Its cathedral is the largest neo-Gothic church in the Americas, finished in 1999 after 114 years.
santa-rosa: For St Rose of Lima, the first saint born in the Americas.
The capital of La Pampa, founded in 1892 by a rancher on his own land.
The Parque Luro nearby preserves a patch of caldén forest, the pampas’ only native woodland.
tandil: From a Mapudungun word, possibly "falling stone", for a balancing rock that stood above the town.
That rock, the Piedra Movediza, fell in 1912; a replica now stands in its place.
The town is known nationwide for its salami and cheese, and its hills are among the oldest rock in South America.
mar-del-plata: "Sea of the Plata" — the seaside counterpart to the river name.
Argentina’s main beach resort, where Buenos Aires goes in January.
Its film festival is the only competitive one in Latin America recognised by the international federation.
bahia-blanca: "White bay", for the salt flats around its harbour.
It is the main deep-water port of the southern pampas and ships much of Argentina’s grain.
Its naval base at Puerto Belgrano is the largest in the country.
comodoro-rivadavia: Named for a naval commodore, Martín Rivadavia.
Argentine oil was discovered here by accident in 1907 by men drilling for water.
It is the windiest city in the country, and the wind is now farmed for electricity.
